justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline for the S&P 500 across all three horizons, anchored around the 516–522 range on the SPY ETF. At the one-day horizon, I leaned on mean-reversion tendencies and the absence of major scheduled catalysts to place the estimate near recent closing levels with minimal drift. At the one-week horizon, I incorporated a slight upward bias reflecting the broader trend of resilient earnings and still-accommodative financial conditions, while acknowledging that intraday noise can compound over several sessions. At the one-month horizon, the modest additional drift reflects a continuation of the prevailing slow grind higher that equity markets have exhibited, tempered by the recognition that valuations are stretched and macro surprises could easily reverse near-term gains.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to historical realized volatility for SPY at each time horizon. Daily SPY moves of roughly 0.5–1% are typical in a low-volatility regime, which produces the relatively tight 19-point band at one day. Over a week, volatility scales with the square root of time, widening the band to 36 points, and over a month it widens further to 68 points. I also gave some additional weight to the possibility of volatility clustering — if conditions turn volatile, moves can be larger than the square-root-of-time rule suggests, which is reflected in the intervals being slightly asymmetric on the downside.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include a sudden shift in Federal Reserve communication — particularly any surprise dovish or hawkish pivot — which historically causes outsized single-day moves in equities. Geopolitical escalation, a credit event in commercial real estate or regional banking, or an unexpected inflation print could all generate moves beyond the 90% confidence bands, especially at the one-month horizon. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected resolution to trade tensions or a surprise rate cut could similarly breach the upper bound.

It is worth emphasizing that these intervals capture roughly 90% of plausible outcomes under relatively normal market conditions, meaning tail events — however low probability — remain real possibilities. The one-month interval in particular should be treated with humility, as macro regimes can shift meaningfully over four weeks and historical volatility is an imperfect guide to future uncertainty.
